articles.title: Important Changes to the 2024 ERP Boot Camp
articles.content:
We are disappointed to announce that we will not be holding a regular 10-day ERP Boot Camp this summer.

We have held Boot Camps nearly every summer since 2007, supported by a series of generous grants from NIMH that allowed us to provide scholarships for all attendees. Unfortunately, although our recent renewal proposal received extremely positive reviews and scores, we were recently given the surprising and disappointing news that the renewal will not be funded this year. We believe that the ERP Boot Camp provides essential training to the field, and we will continue to pursue financial support to continue holding 10-day ERP Boot Camps in the future.

In the meantime, we have partial funding that will allow us to hold a 5-day ERP Boot Camp this summer from July 8-12, 2024 in Davis, California. The workshop will include 5-days of lectures and activities on EEG and ERP measures, including practical and theoretical issues.

Unfortunately, we will not be able to provide scholarships to pay for travel and lodging costs, and we must charge a registration fee. We are very sorry if this causes a hardship.

We are no longer taking applications through our application portal. Instead of a competitive application process, we will simply accept the first 30 people who complete the registration process and pay the registration fee. This provides an opportunity to attend for individuals who might otherwise not make it through our ordinary application process, which is highly competitive.

The registration fee will be $1000 (or $900 for people who register by April 15). The registration fee will cover 6 nights in a single occupancy hotel room (arriving July 7 and departing July 13), daily breakfast at the hotel, a catered lunch for each day of the workshop, and a group dinner. You must pay the registration fee with a credit card when you register. There are no exceptions to the registration fee policy.

Registration is now open at https://na.eventscloud.com/793175.

Given that we will accept the first 30 registrants, we encourage you to register as soon as possible. Registration will close on May 20, but we anticipate that the workshop will be filled up long before then.

You must pay for your own transportation to Davis. Davis is approximately 20 minutes away from the Sacramento Airport (SMF). You can take the Davis Airporter shuttle service or a rideshare service from SMF to Davis. If you are coming from outside North America, you may want to fly into the San Francisco airport (SFO), which is 135 km (84 miles) from Davis. We recommend taking the Davis Airporter from SFO to Davis.

articles.title: Standardized Measurement Error now available in BrainVision Analyzer and MNE-Python
articles.content:
A few years ago, we developed a universal metric of data quality for averaged ERPs called the standardized measurement error (click here for more information or watch our quick 3-minute video overview). It has been available in ERPLAB for several years, and I’m happy to announce that it is now available in BrainVision Analyzer 2.3.1 and in MNE-Python.

For BrainVision Analyzer, it is available as a Solution. At this point, you need to request it from Brain Products. Click here and scroll down to the last part of the page for more information.

For MNE-Python, it is accessed with the mne.stats.erp.compute_sme() function. Click here for details.

If you want to see some examples of how this metric can be used, check out these recent papers:

  • Zhang, G., Garrett, D. R., & Luck, S. J. (2024a). Optimal filters for ERP research I: A general approach for selecting filter settings. Psychophysiology, 61, e14531. http://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14531 [preprint]

  • Zhang, G., Garrett, D. R., & Luck, S. J. (2024b). Optimal filters for ERP research II: Recommended settings for seven common ERP components. Psychophysiology, 61, e14530. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14530 [preprint]

  • Zhang, G., Garrett, D. R., Simmons, A. M., Kiat, J. E., & Luck, S. J. (2024). Evaluating the effectiveness of artifact correction and rejection in event-related potential research. Psychophysiology, 61, e14511. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14511 [preprint]

  • Zhang, G., & Luck, S. J. (2023). Variations in ERP data quality across paradigms, participants, and scoring procedures. Psychophysiology, 60, e14264. http://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14264 [preprint]

articles.author: Deidre Artis

articles.title: Short-Term Plasticity of Contrast Surround Suppression During Repeated Psychophysical Measurement
articles.content: Perceptual surround suppression is commonly treated as stable within a testing session, but recent evidence for normalization reweighting suggests that suppressive interactions can be modified by recent visual input. Here, we asked whether surround suppression changes over minutes of repeated measurement and whether such change varies with stimulus and sampling conditions. Across four psychophysical experiments, we tracked contrast and motion surround suppression while varying center-surround orientation and stimulus spatiotemporal properties. With static gratings, contrast surround suppression increased early and then approached a plateau, with no evidence that this change depended on center-surround orientation. With dynamic gratings, an increase emerged only under finer temporal sampling and more sustained stimulation, and model-based analyses suggested a faster increase than with static stimulation. Motion surround suppression measured with drifting gratings showed no systematic change. Together, these findings show that contrast surround suppression can change within a single psychophysical session without a separate adaptation phase, and that its measured time course varies with stimulus and sampling conditions. The results are consistent with rapid, experience-dependent reweighting of contextual normalization.
articles.author: Jin, N., Zhang, Q., Cai, Y.

articles.title: Dishevelled2 Condensates control Axon Initial Segment (AIS) assembly and function through MTCL1-Dependent microtubule recruitment.
articles.content: In the epithelium, Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) signaling coordinates cellular organization along the plane of the tissue, perpendicular to the apicobasal axis. In neurons, polarity is instead expressed through the structural and molecular asymmetry that separates the axon from the somatodendritic compartment. Core PCP proteins are essential for neuronal development and function, and have been linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism spectrum disorders and epilepsy. However, their precise roles in the establishment of neuronal polarity remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify Dishevelled2 (Dvl2), a central PCP signaling scaffold, as a novel component of the axon initial segment (AIS), the proximal axonal domain that maintains neuronal polarity and initiates action potentials. We show that Dvl2 defines, both in vivo and in cultured hippocampal neurons, a proximal subdomain positioned upstream of the major AIS marker Ankyrin-G (Ank-G) and is closely associated with microtubule bundles. Dvl2 is already detected during early axon specification, suggesting that it participates in the initial organization of the proximal axon. Functional depletion of Dvl proteins disrupts AIS architecture, reduces the accumulation of Ankyrin-G and other core AIS components, and impairs the organization of AIS microtubule bundles. These structural defects translate into altered neuronal excitability, with a reduced AIS-dependent component of the action potential. Mechanistically, we identify MTCL1 as a microtubule-associated partner that recruits Dvl2 from biomolecular condensate assemblies onto microtubules. This recruitment requires the DIX and PDZ domains of Dvl2. Notably, selective intracellular binders targeting the Dvl2 PDZ domain perturb Dvl2 condensate organization and compromise AIS formation. Together, our data identify Dvl2 as an organizer of the proximal AIS and reveal a Dvl2-MTCL1-dependent mechanism coupling condensate scaffolding, microtubule organization, and neuronal excitability.

articles.title: Concurrent anodal tDCS enhances motor learning and increases cortical TrkB phosphorylation
articles.content: The timing of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) relative to motor practice may influence its behavioral effects, but the accompanying molecular responses remain incompletely characterized. Here, we examined cortical current delivery, rotarod performance, and BDNF-TrkB signaling in mice receiving anodal tDCS concurrently with training or during intertrial intervals. Cortical current measurements indicated that approximately half of the applied current reached the measurement site under the experimental stimulation configuration. During four days of rotarod training, anodal tDCS concurrent with motor tasks improved performance at selected trials and increased footstep frequency, whereas stimulation delivered before or after training trials did not significantly improve performance. Preceding online anodal tDCS with cathodal stimulation provided no detectable additional behavioral benefit. Concurrent anodal tDCS increased TrkB phosphorylation in the stimulated cortex after both one and four days, without a significant increase in BDNF levels. Paused offline anodal tDCS stimulation also increased TrkB phosphorylation after one day despite lacking a detectable behavioral benefit. No significant molecular changes were detected in the sampled non-targeted brain regions. Genetic experiments revealed reduced rotarod performance in BDNF heterozygous mice at several trials and trial-dependent responses to online stimulation in BDNF-KIV mice. Together, these findings show that concurrent anodal tDCS improves rotarod performance and increases TrkB phosphorylation in the stimulated cortex. These results motivate further investigation of how BDNF-TrkB signaling interacts with task-related neural activity during stimulation.
articles.author: Wang, Y., Yu, Q., Wen, Y.

articles.title: Movie Watching for Individual Functional Brain Network Estimation in Adolescents
articles.content: Precision functional mapping (PFM) reveals stable individual differences in brain functional network organization and holds promise for advancing neuropsychiatric clinical care. PFM requires sufficient high-quality and densely-sampled functional MRI data at the individual level that is typically acquired during the so-called resting state while passively fixating on a crosshair. However, crosshair fixation acquisitions can be challenging especially for pediatric or patient populations, where alternatives like movie watching might be used to improve data quality and reduce participant burden. Here, we compare the use of resting state crosshair fixation and movie watching fMRI data to derive individual-specific functional brain network topography using PFM data (28-38 minutes of low-motion fMRI data per-participant per-condition) in nineteen adolescents (12-18 years) with a range of transdiagnostic psychiatric diagnoses. Network assignments were largely conserved between crosshair fixation and movie watching, with a smaller subset of reproducible network reassignments which were overwhelmingly border shifts between neighboring networks. This suggests largely conserved global structure of functional network topography between crosshair fixation and movie watching, though border shifts can compound into variable estimates of cortical network size particularly for movie positive (language, salience, and parietal memory) and movie negative networks (default mode, action mode). Functional network assignments derived from movies and crosshair were also similarly individual-specific and consistent within common neuromodulation targets including dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and somatomotor cortex. Key results were replicated in independent pediatric consortia data (Healthy Brain Network, n = 466, 6-22 years) and reproduced across independent PFM data sessions. Acknowledging individual differences and level of analysis, we conclude that movies are a viable alternative to resting state crosshair fixation for individual network definitions.

articles.title: Time at Home for Whom? Unequal Returns of Paid Family Leave for Infant White Matter and Language Development
articles.content: Paid family leave (PFL) may give parents more time with infants, ease financial strain, and support stable routines. Although PFL has been linked to child development, little is known about neural pathways that might underpin its benefits or whether associations vary across families. Using data from 274 infants in the HEALthy Brain and Child Development Study, we examined associations of maternal and paternal PFL with language ability at 12 months and white matter microstructure at 6 months. We tested whether associations varied by the corresponding parent's education. Neither maternal nor paternal PFL was directly associated with language scores or fractional anisotropy in the left arcuate, inferior longitudinal, or uncinate fasciculus. Maternal education moderated associations between maternal PFL and fractional anisotropy in the arcuate (p = .014) and inferior longitudinal fasciculus (p = .003; n = 148). In both tracts, PFL was associated with higher fractional anisotropy only among infants whose mothers had relatively high education. No comparable pattern emerged for language, the uncinate fasciculus, or paternal PFL. Findings suggest that the neurodevelopmental correlates of PFL may depend on family resources rather than operate uniformly across families, underscoring the need to pair paid leave with additional supports and resources.
articles.author: Lazarus, M. F., Nelson, C. A.

articles.title: Neurobiological alterations and autism-like phenotype in mice following regulatory-limit exposure to fungicides in drinking water
articles.content: Neurodevelopmental conditions, including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorders (ASD), have increased markedly over recent decades. This rise parallels the widespread use of agrochemicals, suggesting a contribution of environmental exposures. We hypothesize that pesticide residues may disrupt brain development and promote neurodevelopmental disorders. Here, we test whether concentrations permitted in drinking water affect brain development using a maternal exposure model in wild-type mice. Exposure to a fungicide mixture at 0.3 g/L, below the current European regulatory limit of 0.5 g/L, impairs corticogenesis and is associated with alterations in synaptic function and glutamatergic signaling. Offspring exhibit delays in sensory development, reduced social interactions, and increased stereotyped behaviors. We identify the adenosine A2A receptor as a molecular target of anilinopyrimidine fungicides. Together, these findings indicate that low-dose exposure to this fungicide mixture can induce an autism spectrum-like phenotype in the offspring.

articles.title: Cross Study Regulator Activity Analysis Reveals Convergent Programs in alpha Synuclein PFF Models of Parkinson Disease
articles.content: Alpha-synuclein preformed fibril (PFF) models reproduce features of Parkinson disease (PD), but differences in brain region, cell composition, and experimental design complicate comparisons across studies. We reconstructed study-specific regulatory networks using ARACNe (Algorithm for the Reconstruction of Accurate Cellular Networks) and inferred transcription factor (TF) and transcription cofactor activity using VIPER (Virtual Inference of Protein-activity by Enriched Regulon analysis). Five transcriptomic comparisons from four mouse PFF datasets were analyzed, with human PD single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data used to assess cross-species agreement. In the dopamine-neuron-enriched dataset GSE252967, PFF exposure was associated with increased activity of stress- and inflammation-related TFs, including JUND and RELA, and decreased activity of dopaminergic-identity regulators, including NR4A2, LMX1B, FOXA1, FOXA2, PITX3, and EN1. Several regulators were connected to Th in the inferred network. The substantia nigra bulk dataset GSE296779 showed reduced activity of ATF4- and XBP1-associated protein homeostasis and unfolded protein response programs, supported by regulon-weighted gene-set enrichment. Supporting mouse comparisons showed limited overlap in individual TFs but identified changes in inflammatory, glial, and stress-related programs. Agreement between inferred activity and transcript-level changes ranged from 64% to 100% in these comparisons. Human PD data showed cell-type-dependent agreement with mouse findings. EN1 and PITX3 were shared between the mouse and human networks upstream of Th/TH and showed reduced inferred activity in all seven human cell types, alongside nonsignificant decreases in the mouse dataset. These analyses identified changes in dopaminergic-identity, protein homeostasis, and inflammatory transcriptional programs across mouse PFF models, with partial support in human PD.
articles.author: Tang, Y., Xiao, A., Xiao, Y., Li, R., Huang, Z., Wang, A., li, L., Khan, M. M.

articles.title: Tasting from memory: reconstructing taste from visual cues in the human brain
articles.content: Taste guides us toward nourishment and away from harm. Yet when we decide what to eat, taste only exists in memory, evoked by a cue. How the brain retrieves taste memories is almost entirely unknown. If memory re-creates experience, it should reproduce the brain's activation while tasting, even in the absence of taste. We scanned participants while they formed and then retrieved associations between tastes and visual cues. The gustatory cortex was engaged during retrieval and distinguished among remembered tastes, but not using the patterns it had formed while tasting. Patterns persisted instead in lateral parietal cortex, distinguishing individual tastes, not just taste-categories. Activity in the amygdala covaried with this same parietal region and amygdala activity predicted which associations were retained. Taste memory is not simply a re-creation of sensory experience, but a distinct representation, outside the taste system, yet specific enough to guide what we choose to eat.

articles.title: A parsimonious, age-invariant, and psychometrically validated neural signature of task-control network functioning
articles.content: Neuroimaging has vast potential for identifying brain features that support individual and developmental differences in cognition, but challenges related to the dimensionality, unreliability, and unknown developmental properties of neuroimaging measures prevent this from being realized. We overcome these challenges by applying latent variable modeling to demand-related responses in the "task-control" frontoparietal and dorsal attention networks (FPN, DAN) within the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study and Human Connectome Project. Task-control activations are well-captured by a bifactor structure with a general factor spanning FPN/DAN and network-specific factors that is remarkably invariant across middle childhood to early adolescence and largely generalizes to adulthood. Trait-state-occasion modeling reveals a general task-control trait that shows robust associations with cognitive abilities, clinical symptoms, and grades. Repeated neuroimaging substantially increases associations. Findings establish a parsimonious neural signature that generalizes across samples, is stable across development, and has broad utility for understanding developmental and individual differences in goal-directed behavior.
articles.author: Paige, K. J., Molloy, M. F., Angstadt, M., Hyde, L., Sripada, C., Heitzeg, M., Weigard, A. J.

articles.title: Dynamics of dopamine transients in human olfactory epithelium during reward learning
articles.content: Dopamine signaling is crucial for motivation, movement, and learning, but has remained beyond the reach of measurement in healthy humans. Here, we measured sub-second dopamine in the olfactory epithelium of healthy humans during two reward learning tasks with distinct reward types: liquid reward during a conditioning task and monetary reward during an economic exchange game. In both tasks, as trials progress, peak dopamine transients shift from rewarding outcomes back to reward-predictive cues. In the economic game, this pattern retrains quickly when reward magnitude or reward timing is changed without warning. These findings match the time transfer characteristics and amplitude dependence of temporal difference prediction error signals. The results also establish a new, minimally invasive route for recording fast dopamine signaling in healthy humans: the nose.
